transcript: Just this week, The Public is presenting a brief run of When The Hurlyburly’s Done by Richard Nelson. This play is about six women in Ukraine in 1920 during the Ukrainian War of Independence. These women are actors and dancers, and their art is what feeds them creatively and literally. This production, performed in Ukrainian and captioned in English, is very intimate and conversational, focusing on showing us the lives of these characters at this specific point in time as opposed to telling a neat and tidy story. These women discuss and work on their Shakespeare plays, they cook, they eat, they worry, they grieve, they wait. Wartime is obviously hard, and for these characters, much of it is spent thinking about their purpose within these circumstances. They mostly find meaning in their children, their art, and each other. This play is extremely relevant right now, and everyone in the audience felt the weight of it, especially during the absolute gut punch of a finale. But part of the beauty of this play is also how it highlights laughter and art in spite of everything that tries to stifle it. It's about how creativity is something that not even a war can take from us, and how it's arguably under that kind of circumstance when our creativity is most vital. I'm really grateful I got to see this. A line that'll stay with me is “sometimes I walk on stage and all is forgotten.” With that, another program for my collection.
